Who runs the PJM grid, and what is its capacity market called?
answer: PJM Interconnection runs the PJM grid (docs/grids/pjm.md, written text). It runs the largest wholesale electricity market in the United States. It covers all or part of thirteen states and the District of Columbia. PJM owns no power plants. It schedules its members' plants, keeps supply equal to demand, and plans the high-voltage transmission lines. FERC approves its market rules. Its capacity market is called the Reliability Pricing Model (RPM), and PJM runs an RPM auction each year (docs/grids/pjm.md).

question: What makes SPP different from other grids, and how much wind did it generate over the last 7 days you hold?
first_answer:
What makes SPP different: wind. The Great Plains are among the windiest places in the country. On windy nights wind can supply a large share of SPP's power, which pushes some prices to zero or below. The wind is far from cities, so delivery depends on long transmission lines. SPP curtails wind when those lines are full (docs/grids/spp.md, written text, not data). SPP also owns no power plants, and it has no capacity auction. Its members must show they have enough capacity themselves (docs/grids/spp.md).

Wind over the last 7 days held: the newest SPP (SWPP) hour in the warehouse is 2026-09-27 23:00 UTC. I used the 7 UTC days 2026-09-21 00:00 to 2026-09-28 00:00 UTC, which is 168 hourly values. Wind net generation averaged 10363.67 MW (mean of the 168 hourly values, eia930_all_generation). The hourly values sum to 1741096 MW-hours, i.e. about 1.74 million MWh (eia930_all_generation). The last hour, 2026-09-27 23:00 UTC, was 3952 MW (eia930_all_generation). Times are UTC. Central time is UTC-5 in September.
